summary: Discusses problems with NAT-PT, the IPv6-to-IPv4 translation mechanism defined in RFC 2766. The problems are serious enough that it should no longer be recommended as a general transition tool, and the document recommends reclassifying RFC 2766 as Historic. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: NAT-PT translates traffic between IPv4-only and IPv6-only systems. This RFC explains why the translation and its DNS helper cause problems and recommends against using NAT-PT as a general transition mechanism.

subtitle: Why the RFC recommends against using NAT-PT as a general IPv4-to-IPv6 transition tool.

tldr.problem: NAT-PT was designed to let IPv4-only and IPv6-only nodes communicate, but translation and DNS-ALG behavior create technical, operational and security problems.
tldr.mechanism: The memo groups the problems into those independent of DNS-ALG, those worsened by it and those caused directly by its DNS rewriting.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4966 concludes that the problems make NAT-PT unsuitable as a general transition mechanism and recommends moving RFC 2766 to Historic status.

today: RFC 4966 is an Informational memo that obsoletes RFC 2766. It recommends that RFC 2766 be moved to Historic status and that NAT-PT no longer be suggested as a general transition mechanism.

sections.title: What NAT-PT Was Intended to Do
sections.content:
RFC 2766 defines the Network Address Translator - Protocol Translator (NAT-PT) to let IPv4-only nodes communicate with IPv6-only nodes. Basic NAT-PT translates addresses; NAPT-PT also translates transport identifiers. Both use the Stateless IP/ICMP Translation Algorithm (SIIT) described in RFC 2765.

RFC 4966 reviews problems raised by earlier documents and adds concerns from traditional IPv4 NATs. It treats the DNS application layer gateway (DNS-ALG) as part of NAT-PT because the simpler case without it was not worked out in RFC 2766.
sections.plainLanguage: NAT-PT changes packet information so an IPv4-only system can communicate with an IPv6-only system. The memo reviews problems with that translation design and its DNS helper.

sections.title: Problems Independent of the DNS Helper
sections.content:
Protocols that include IP addresses in their data may need a separate helper to rewrite those addresses. Encryption or integrity checks can prevent a translator from changing packet contents. IPv4 and IPv6 also differ in information they carry, and fragments after the first do not include port numbers needed by NAPT-PT.

The RFC also discusses state timeouts that can break idle connections, problems redirecting protocols without a visible port, limitations involving SCTP multihoming and Mobile IPv6, and the inability of SIIT to translate multicast packets. These issues apply beyond NAT-PT to network-layer IPv4/IPv6 translators generally.
sections.plainLanguage: Translation can fail when a protocol hides addresses inside its data, relies on encrypted contents, or carries information that has no match in the other IP version. Fragmentation, idle bindings, mobility and multicast create additional problems.

sections.title: Problems Made Worse by DNS-ALG
sections.content:
The DNS-ALG must see queries that need translated addresses, which constrains where NAT-PT sits in the network. The memo says this can make the translator the site's default IPv6 router, send traffic through a bottleneck and create a single point of failure.

Translated address mappings may expire before applications use them or may not persist between sessions. Queries can also create bindings without authentication, potentially exhausting the translator's memory and address or port pools. The RFC notes that cooperating translators would require state coordination that had not been standardized.
sections.plainLanguage: The DNS helper has to see name lookups that need translation, which can force traffic through the translator. That concentrates traffic and state in one place, where failures or excess requests can disrupt service.

sections.title: Problems Caused by DNS Rewriting
sections.content:
The DNS-ALG rewrites DNS responses to provide translated addresses. A dual-stack host may choose a translated address instead of a native IPv6 address, and another application may receive a translated answer that only works through that particular NAT-PT. A stateless DNS-ALG may also translate an answer to an IPv4 A query into a synthesized AAAA record.

When a host has several addresses, the DNS-ALG may create bindings for all of them. Rewriting DNS responses invalidates DNSSEC signatures, so the RFC concludes DNSSEC cannot be deployed in domains using NAT-PT as specified.
sections.plainLanguage: Rewritten DNS answers may direct a system to an address that only works through one translator. The rewriting also invalidates DNSSEC signatures on those answers.

sections.title: Recommendation and Application Effects
sections.content:
The RFC warns that applications may not know a NAT-PT is on the path, so assumptions about native IPv6 can fail. Making every application work around a temporary translator would also constrain IPv6 application development.

Some fixes would require major specification changes and add operational complexity, while other problems remain. The memo recommends that the IETF stop suggesting NAT-PT as a general IPv4-IPv6 transition mechanism and move RFC 2766 from Proposed Standard to Historic status. It allows that a more limited translator could suit constrained situations.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors recommend retiring NAT-PT as a general transition tool because problems remain even if some issues are fixed. A narrower translation design might still suit a limited situation.
